title: How to make a password a hacker can't crack
description:
A hacker's graphics card can guess about 100 billion passwords a second against a fast hash like MD5. Eight random lowercase letters (26 to the 8th, 209 billion options) fall in 2 seconds; adding capitals, digits and symbols (95 choices per spot) only buys 18 hours. Length wins: every extra letter multiplies the work by 26, so 16 random letters take 14,000 years to try in full. Six words picked with dice from the 7,776-word Diceware list take 70,000 years, and you can remember them.

Numbers checked in code (exact counts and a 100,000-trial brute-force simulation). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diceware https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Password_cracking https://hashcat.net/forum/post-57490.html

The math behind real problems, twice a day. Subscribe and the next one finds you.

facts_checked: One RTX 4090 runs ~150 billion MD5 guesses/s in hashcat; the video uses 100 billion/s (https://hashcat.net/forum/post-57490.html)
26^8 = 208.8 billion -> 2 s to try all at 100 billion/s (verify.py)
Diceware: 7,776 = 6^5 words, five dice per word, created by Arnold Reinhold; six words recommended since 2014 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diceware)
Dictionary attacks and common-password checks are usually tried before brute force (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Password_cracking)
CTA: 5 dice words (~9 years) beat 12 random letters (11 days), ~300x more options (verify.py)
Brute force on average searches half the space (100,000-trial simulation in verify.py)

beats.say: You're making a new password, and a hacker's graphics card can guess 100 billion a second. Here's how you beat it.
First, count what it has to try. 8 lowercase letters: 26 choices for every spot.
Multiply 26 by itself 8 times: 209 billion passwords. At 100 billion a second, that's 2 seconds.
So add capitals, digits and symbols. Now every spot has 95 choices. That's 6.6 quadrillion, and it falls in 18 hours.
Better. Now make it longer instead. Every extra letter multiplies the work by 26. 12 letters: 11 days. 16 letters: 14,000 years.
So use words. Take a list of 7,776 words, and roll five dice to pick each one.
Now every word multiplies the work by 7,776. Six random words: 70,000 years. And you can still remember them.
But let the dice pick. Hackers try real phrases and common passwords first, long before random ones.
And there you have it: a password you can remember, that outlasts the hacker by 70,000 years.
This is Diceware. Arnold Reinhold made the list, and he now says to use at least six words.
So, 5 random words, or 12 random letters. Which takes longer to crack?
